title: Grade 8 Math — Mon, May 18
description: Rational Numbers — Day 1 of 5: What are rational numbers?
subject: mathematics

questions.question: A rational number is a number that can be written as:
options: p/q where p, q are integers and q ≠ 0
questions.explanation: Rational number: p/q form, where p and q are integers (positive, negative, or zero) and q ≠ 0. Examples: 3/4, -5/2, 7 (=7/1), 0.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a rational number?
questions.explanation: √2 cannot be expressed as p/q (it is irrational). 3/4, −7/2, and 0 (=0/1) are all rational.

questions.question: Is every integer a rational number?
questions.explanation: Every integer n can be written as n/1, which is p/q form. So all integers are rational numbers.

questions.question: The rational number −3/7 is:
questions.explanation: Numerator is negative (−3), denominator is positive (7) → overall negative. −3/7 < 0.

questions.question: Which pair represents the SAME rational number?
questions.explanation: −4/6 = −2/3 (divide both by 2). Equivalent fractions represent the same rational number.

questions.question: Rational numbers between 0 and 1:
questions.explanation: Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many rationals. Between 0 and 1: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 2/3, 3/4... infinite.

questions.question: Represent −5/3 on the number line. It lies:
questions.explanation: −5/3 = −1.666... It lies between −1 and −2 on the number line.

questions.question: The additive inverse of 3/7 is:
questions.explanation: Additive inverse of p/q is −p/q. Additive inverse of 3/7 = −3/7. (Note: 3/−7 = −3/7 are the same.)

questions.question: The multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of −4/9 is:
questions.explanation: Multiplicative inverse of p/q is q/p. Inverse of −4/9 = 9/−4 = −9/4.

questions.question: Which property says: a/b + 0 = a/b?
questions.explanation: Identity property of addition: adding 0 doesn't change a number. 0 is the additive identity for rational numbers.

questions.question: Which property says: a/b × 1 = a/b?
questions.explanation: 1 is the multiplicative identity: any rational number multiplied by 1 stays unchanged.

questions.question: Is the set of rational numbers closed under addition?
options: No — the sum may be irrational
Yes — sum of two rationals is always rational
Only if they have the same denominator
questions.explanation: Closure under addition: p/q + r/s = (ps+qr)/qs — still p/q form (rational). Yes, closed.

questions.question: Is the set of rational numbers closed under division?
options: No — division by zero is undefined; otherwise yes
questions.explanation: Rational ÷ rational = rational, EXCEPT division by zero is undefined. So rational numbers are closed under division excluding division by 0.

questions.question: Find two rational numbers between 1/4 and 1/2:
questions.explanation: 1/4 = 3/12, 1/2 = 6/12. Between them: 4/12 = 1/3 and 5/12. Both lie between 1/4 and 1/2.

questions.question: Summary: rational numbers are best described as:
options: All numbers expressible as p/q (integers p, q; q≠0) — includes integers, fractions, terminating and repeating decimals
questions.explanation: Rational numbers = p/q form. This includes: all integers, all fractions, and all terminating or repeating decimals (like 0.5=1/2, 0.333...=1/3).
